cur:objects-vatican-deesis-triptych.summary: In the central panel Christ sits on a richly carved throne with bolster cushions, blessing, while the Virgin and St John the Baptist stand at either side in supplication; further saints stand on the wings in rows. The serene, classically draped figures belong to the most refined group of Constantinopolitan ivories. The triptych places the viewer before the heavenly court, with Christ enthroned as Judge and Saviour.
facts: The Deesis — Christ between the interceding Virgin and John the Baptist — is the central theme of several of the finest 10th-century Constantinopolitan ivory triptychs, among them the Harbaville Triptych in the Louvre (comparison).

Q116276416.summary: This tiny gold clasp holds at its centre a beaded medallion incised with the Virgin, her head veiled and haloed, and the Christ Child in a roundel before her breast, flanked by small crosses. Designed to be worn, it expressed its owner's devotion to Mary as Theotokos, the Mother of God, who bears Christ to the world.
facts: An inscription on the reverse, according to the Met, expresses the owner's devotion to the Virgin as Theotokos.
The Met notes that crosses appear on Byzantine jewellery by the 5th century, while images of the Virgin, saints and angels became popular in the 6th.
It was a gift of Helen Miller Gould in 1910.
Q116276416.notes: The Child is very small in the medallion; his presence is visible in the photograph. The inscription is not transcribed.
